title: the audit head signed hourly, an anchor folder the box's root can write over refused (plan 10 row 10G-2)
note: No box, share or Docker daemon here. The refusals are shown on stand-ins (read-only files and folders, a non-root account, the kernel's own answers) and with each probe's answer replaced; the cron lines on a temporary cron folder.

findings.claim: The first judgement asked only whether the newest head could be overwritten (access(2)), not whether a head could be deleted or renamed: a share that refuses an overwrite but allows a delete let the box's root delete a head and write another in its place. The rework judges overwrite of the head just written, and rename, delete and overwrite of a test file in heads/

The root-proof judgement has not been run on a real anchor folder (the hospital's share with root squashed and create-only rights, or a WORM share): it is shown on stand-ins only. The first box's install shows it: an anchor on the box's own disk must make audit-sign exit 1 with 'cannot be root-proof' (PRODUCTION: no head written there), and a passing share must leave heads/.root-probe in place

doctor cannot judge the anchor folders itself: check_host.sh mounts them read-only into the image, where every write is refused. It reads the last hourly run's result (its folder now mounted, a missing result a FAIL), so a folder that stopped being root-proof is a FAIL at most one run later, not at once

The audit signing key is wrapped under the same KEK that adapter and orchestrator (uid 10001) hold for their own keys, and they mount the secrets volume: the private audit key's file permissions (root's, 0600, doctor audit_key_root) are the only barrier between those services and a signed head. A real separation needs the audit key under a KEK of its own that only the signer can open, or the key off the box (an HSM, or heads signed by the hospital)
